rule: Read claims/RULES.md. Exhaustively enumerate atomic candidate facts in the frozen raw_response, without checking truth. Exclude question restatements, recommendations and explicit uncertainty from facts; inventory uncertainties separately. Give an exact source_quote for every item. Map an actually supplied URL when present, distinguishing homepage_only, claim_specific and none. citation_links recovers the address of a citation actually printed in that response; it is not new evidence. Preserve any unresolved citation refs separately. Do not infer facts from external knowledge or from the query/document logs. Deduplicate repeated facts within a run. Return reviewed_runs, facts, uncertainties and omissions/limits. No gold or other files.

I would evaluate LEMON first, then compare SNAP and NetworKit against the actual mix of graph lookups, traversals, and edits. OGDF is a reasonable additional option when its graph algorithms or drawing capabilities matter and its license is acceptable. LLAMA offers a different storage mechanism worth considering when the workload consists of updates followed by substantial analysis.

This is a ranked research shortlist, not a performance result. I did not build these libraries or test them on a graph with the specified degree distribution. In particular, support for adding or deleting an edge does not establish that deletion from a very high-degree vertex will be inexpensive.

1. LEMON — ListDigraph/ListGraph and alternative graph representations
   https://lemon.cs.elte.hu/pub/doc/1.3.1/a00244.html
   Supporting overview: https://lemon.cs.elte.hu/pub/tutorial/a00015.html

   This is the closest structural match in the evidence I examined. Its directed ListDigraph and undirected ListGraph support additions and removals, while the tutorial also describes changing endpoints and contracting or splitting graph elements. The graph concepts provide iterators and maps for attaching data. ListGraph stores linked-list relationships inside vectors and offers reservation operations, which makes it particularly relevant to the concern about excessive separate allocations. The same library exposes different tradeoffs: Smart representations provide less mutation flexibility, and StaticDigraph targets a graph built once and then traversed.

   Those choices are not interchangeable. Smart variants cannot delete arbitrary elements, and StaticDigraph cannot be updated. The ListGraph reference describes iterator invalidation and the possible reuse of removed identifiers. The numbered documentation was accessible, but the project front page and documentation index were blocked, so I have left its exact historical date and full dependency/license verification unresolved rather than backdating the live material.

2. SNAP — Stanford Network Analysis Platform
   https://snap.stanford.edu/snap-1.8/doc.html
   Historical evidence: https://github.com/snap-stanford/snap/blob/master/Release.txt

   SNAP is attractive when the graph is also a network-analysis object. Its tutorial documents directed, undirected, and directed multigraph families, as well as network classes parameterized by node and edge data. It provides explicit node identifiers, iterators, subgraph operations, and compact network types. The TBigNet description specifically addresses fragmentation. Historical release entries establish attributed-network support before March 2016.

   The main integration caveat is its use of GLib, its own STL-like vectors, hashes, pointer types, and conventions. That is a substantial API choice to evaluate if modern C++ style is important. Its release history also records incompatible changes and mutation-related fixes, so I would pin a version and inspect invalidation and deletion semantics. The sources establish relevant functionality, not measured performance for this workload.

3. NetworKit C++ core
   https://networkit.github.io/
   Historical evidence: https://networkit.github.io/news.html

   NetworKit is worth testing when efficient traversal and scalable analysis are major requirements. The current project documentation describes a native C++ core with many parallel algorithms. Dated release notes establish directed graph support in July 2014, arbitrary edge attributes through indexing in August 2014, and directed-to-undirected conversion in the 2014 series. The history also contains support for power-law degree sequences, which is relevant to generating a demanding test workload, without proving that all operations handle degree skew efficiently.

   Its public presentation emphasizes analytics and Python integration, so the exact native integration and graph mutation API deserve examination. I have not verified the cost of every insertion/removal, the historical C++ standard requirement, or the complete dependency set. Recent templated adjacency-list and Dynamic Hashed Blocks additions are explicitly later evidence and should not be credited to the 2016 version.

4. OGDF — Open Graph Drawing Framework
   https://www.ogdf.uni-osnabrueck.de/
   Design description: https://ogdf.uos.de/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/ogdf.pdf

   OGDF supplies a self-contained C++ core with graph structures, associative arrays for node and edge data, and substantial graph algorithms. Its design chapter is useful evidence for independence from a large external graph framework. It could help an application that needs representation and manipulation alongside planarity, graph decomposition, or drawing.

   The GPL is a material mismatch with the preference for a less restrictive license. Its specialized scope may also be unnecessary for a straightforward graph container. The evidence examined does not justify a claim about low allocation counts or fast arbitrary edits. The official site dates the linked chapter to 2014; the PDF's later upload directory is not used to date the design.

5. LLAMA — multiversioned CSR storage
   https://github.com/goatdb/llama
   License: https://github.com/goatdb/llama/blob/master/LICENSE

   This is a storage-oriented alternative to an ordinary adjacency-list library. LLAMA combines a write-oriented component with CSR-based snapshots and includes node and edge properties. The repository documents C++11 compilation, in-memory configurations, and a permissive three-clause BSD-style license. Its 2015 research references establish the approach before the question date.

   This tradeoff is most interesting when changes arrive between substantial analytical passes over consistent graph views. It requires more integration work than the other candidates. The README warns about unfinished streaming integration and a broken persistent deletion configuration; I would not assume that every directed/undirected convenience operation or arbitrary edit is available. Its live source revision is not dated by the older research references.

For a practical comparison, I would use the same representative sparse graphs for each candidate and measure neighbor iteration, endpoint lookup, mixed insertion/deletion, edge retargeting or its equivalent, property access, and peak memory. Include high-degree hubs, because average degree can hide expensive local operations. Check which handles and property references survive each edit. That would resolve the performance and stability requirements that documentation alone cannot settle.

Discovery used eight literal searches and fifteen opened-document attempts, including failures and repeat views, leaving four searches and five opens for the separately supplied checks. The unauthenticated grep.app attempt failed; the public repository lookup was explicitly a code-through-web fallback. No recognized exposure to the excluded question thread or its answers occurred.

candidate_links.name: LEMON — ListDigraph/ListGraph with selectable graph representations
LLAMA — mutable multiversioned CSR graph storage

I would start with Fastmail, and put iCloud+ first if everyone in the family mainly uses Apple devices. Infomaniak is worth a trial if an inexpensive provider with its own mobile application matters most. The key ambiguity is whether “native” means an installed application or specifically an interface built with the operating system's native controls: official download availability establishes the former, but does not by itself establish the latter or guarantee that you will find the interface polished.

1. Fastmail — the strongest overall package.
https://www.fastmail.com/pricing/us/
Its observed US plans include Individual at $60/year and Family at $132/year for up to six people, with separate inboxes and custom-domain support. Its official download page currently lists Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS and Android applications: https://www.fastmail.com/download/. This is the first service I would trial against your actual daily email workflow. The material caveat is that these are current, undated pages: I did not establish when the desktop downloads became available or whether they satisfy a strict native-UI requirement.

2. iCloud+ Mail with Apple Mail — especially attractive for an Apple household.
https://www.apple.com/icloud/
The US entry plan is currently $0.99/month, includes custom email domains, and can be shared with five other family members. Mail integrates with Apple's Mail application, which makes this a natural option if the family already uses iPhones, iPads and Macs. Shared iCloud storage also serves photos, files and backups, so select capacity for the household's total usage. Its fit is less automatic for a mixed-platform household. I verified the current product page, but a separate support-page request was rate-limited; historical availability of today's precise offering remains unverified.

3. Infomaniak Mail with Mail Service or kSuite — a lower-cost service with its own mobile apps.
https://www.infomaniak.com/en/ksuite/service-mail/prices
The observed CHF pricing page lists kSuite Standard at CHF 1.76 per user/month and Mail Service from CHF 2.29/month; obtain the actual mailbox and billing configuration before comparing family totals. An official April 13, 2023 announcement confirms iOS and Android apps and links custom-domain email: https://news.infomaniak.com/en/infomaniak-mail-mobile-app/. Be careful to choose the custom-domain offering rather than assuming that a generic-domain personal plan includes it. I have not established a flat family bundle or its own desktop application. Interface quality should be tested with a real mailbox rather than inferred from marketing.

4. Zoho Mail — a budget-oriented option if you tolerate business-style account administration.
https://www.zoho.com/mail/zohomail-pricing.html
Zoho supports custom-domain email with separate users and its own mobile and desktop application options. Its indexed official pricing table showed 5 GB Mail Lite at US$1 per user/month with annual billing, but the opened live page did not expose numeric prices clearly, so treat that amount as provisional until checking the regional quote. Desktop Lite runs on Windows, macOS and Linux but intentionally resembles the web interface: https://www.zoho.com/mail/help/desktop-lite-app.html. The pricing page also advertises Trident as a native macOS/Windows desktop experience; confirm its entitlement on the chosen subscription. No flat household plan was verified.

5. mailbox.org plus Thunderbird or Apple Mail — useful if the application and provider can be chosen separately.
https://mailbox.org/en/prices/
Private Standard currently lists €4/month or €3/month with annual payment, custom domains, and family grouping for up to ten separately charged accounts. The provider explicitly recommends Thunderbird Desktop and documents Apple Mail and IMAP/SMTP compatibility: https://kb.mailbox.org/en/private/faq/compatible-web-browsers/. This lets you judge the native client's interface independently of the hosting provider. It does mean configuring two components, and calendar/contact synchronization can require additional setup. Public code-through-web verification also found the open-source Thunderbird Android project: https://github.com/thunderbird/thunderbird-android/blob/main/README.md.

My practical shortlist is therefore Fastmail for a complete family package, iCloud+ for an Apple household with modest needs, and Infomaniak for a price-sensitive mobile-first trial. Zoho and mailbox.org are conditional alternatives when their account model or separate-client setup is acceptable. These are research-based fit judgments, not hands-on usability results, and none is claimed to have been deployed or proven useful for this household.

Temporal and search limits: the decision cutoff is October 15, 2026. Most opened evidence was live and undated, so I have not backdated today's prices or app availability. Infomaniak's 2023 announcement supports its core mobile offering before the cutoff, not current prices. The required unauthenticated grep.app code-search attempt failed; the public GitHub README was found through web-indexed code instead. For the proxy you describe, I would start with **mitmproxy**. **Fiddler Classic** and **Privoxy** also provide documented ways to change HTML before the browser receives it. For a small experiment without a separate proxy, **Chrome DevTools Local Overrides** is worth considering. If your real requirement is simply to preserve the visible original listing, **SingleFile** offers a different capture workflow.

A qualification matters here: an HTTP proxy receives response content. It can parse and rewrite that HTML, but it does not automatically have the live DOM that the browser constructs after JavaScript runs. Also, the unsuccessful automatic click does not, by itself, establish the cause of the Archiveweb.page recording problem. None of the sources below verifies a fix for this particular eBay interaction.

## Ranked candidates

### 1. mitmproxy

[mitmproxy's feature documentation](https://docs.mitmproxy.org/stable/overview/features/) describes its built-in response-body replacements and support for finer control through scripts. It could help by changing the relevant attribute in the HTML response before the browser parses the page.

For a simple, stable attribute replacement, the built-in replacement mechanism may be enough. If the edit needs to identify a particular element structurally, a Python addon with an HTML parser is a more appropriate approach than a broad regular expression. This does not require adopting Node.js.

For HTTPS, the browser must trust the proxy's certificate authority; see the [certificate documentation](https://docs.mitmproxy.org/stable/concepts/certificates/). Buffered body editing is preferable here: the [public response-modification example](https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/blob/main/examples/addons/http-stream-modify.py) explains why streaming modifications are fragile around chunk boundaries and content lengths.

**Caveat:** Changing the initial HTML will help only if the relevant behavior can be changed there or in another intercepted response. It is not evidence that the archive recorder will capture a later rendered state correctly. The retrieved mitmproxy sources are live and undated, so their precise availability at the question cutoff is unverified.

### 2. Fiddler Classic with FiddlerScript

[Fiddler's response-modification documentation](https://www.telerik.com/fiddler/fiddler-classic/documentation/knowledge-base/fiddlerscript/modifyrequestorresponse) provides a direct match for the requested operation: an OnBeforeResponse rule can decode response content and perform substitutions in HTML before delivery.

This could be useful when you want to inspect traffic and then attach a repeatable rule to the matching host and HTML response. A [dated vendor-team example](https://www.telerik.com/forums/replace-response-textview) demonstrates HTML rewriting through this mechanism in March 2021.

**Caveat:** You would still need to learn the rule syntax and configure HTTPS decryption. This is source-level editing, so it does not supply a browser DOM automatically. The current documentation was updated on October 5, 2026, after the July 14, 2026 cutoff; the separate March 2021 vendor example supports the earlier availability of the underlying mechanism.

### 3. Privoxy content filters

[Privoxy's filter-file manual](https://www.privoxy.org/user-manual/filter-file.html) documents on-the-fly substitutions in HTML and other response text. Its action system can scope those filters to selected URLs, making it a plausible fit for a narrowly targeted attribute change.

The [action manual](https://www.privoxy.org/user-manual/actions-file.html) also describes HTTPS inspection, so current Privoxy is not limited to changing unencrypted pages.

**Caveat:** Its built-in filters use regular expressions against source text. That is convenient for a small stable substitution but fragile for arbitrary nested HTML. HTTPS filtering needs appropriate inspection support and certificate trust. The opened manual identifies version 4.2.0 without establishing its publication date, so I cannot assign this retrieved version to the cutoff date.

### 4. Chrome DevTools Local Overrides

[Chrome's Local Overrides](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/overrides) can replace selected network resources with locally edited content. You can use the Network panel's Override content action, edit the HTML in Sources, save it, and reload. This could test your proposed attribute change without installing a separate interception proxy.

The capability also covers fetch/XHR response content, which may matter if the listing data arrives separately. The [Chrome 117 documentation](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/new-in-devtools-117), dated August 22, 2023, explicitly lists HTML documents and fetch/XHR among the supported resources.

**Caveat:** This substitutes saved resource content; it is less suitable than a proxy rule for transforming many changing listings. Editing an element only in the Elements panel does not create a persistent response override. Whether Archiveweb.page can record successfully with these overrides remains untested.

### 5. SingleFile

[SingleFile](https://github.com/gildas-lormeau/SingleFile) is worth testing if a self-contained HTML copy of the displayed listing meets your archival requirement. Open the original listing, wait until the desired content is visible, and then save the current tab or selected frame.

The relevant difference from your TamperMonkey attempt is the capture workflow: this would save the displayed page using another archiver, rather than asking Archiveweb.page to record an injected click.

**Caveat:** SingleFile is still a browser extension, so it is an alternative to your existing archival workflow rather than the requested proxy. Its HTML snapshot is not equivalent to an interactive WARC/WACZ recording. The [FAQ](https://github.com/gildas-lormeau/SingleFile/blob/main/faq.md) explains that scripts are removed by default and that offline interactive behavior is not guaranteed. The sources opened here are undated live versions, and this exact eBay case has not been tested.

## Practical next step

If maintaining the Archiveweb.page workflow is essential, use mitmproxy or Fiddler to inspect which HTML or data response supplies the original listing, then test one narrowly scoped response change. If a readable record of the listing is sufficient, testing SingleFile after manually revealing it is a smaller experiment. In either case, reopen the resulting archive and check the listing description, images, and any separately loaded frame content before relying on it.

I would start with **SSIS** if you already operate Microsoft SQL Server, and **Astera Centerprise** if you want a dedicated visual ETL product. **FME Form plus FME Flow** is also a credible option for ordinary database tables. EasyMorph and IBM DataStage are worth considering for different team and scale requirements.

Your essential requirement is a complete unattended workflow: connect to the parent database through its supported ODBC driver, select the required tables or rows, transform or consolidate them, load your own database, and record whether the monthly run succeeded. The source and destination database products, data volume, available memory, and support agreement will determine which choice fits best.

### 1. Microsoft SQL Server Integration Services (SSIS) with SQL Server Agent

Microsoft documents ODBC source and destination components that transfer data between databases and connect to SSIS transformation components. The source can extract a table, view, or SQL query result. SQL Server Agent can schedule the package and provide job notifications. This is a strong first evaluation if your team already has SQL Server infrastructure and the skills to maintain packages.

The relevant sources are Microsoft's [ODBC flow documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/integration-services/data-flow/odbc-flow-components?view=sql-server-ver17) and [package scheduling documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/integration-services/packages/sql-server-agent-jobs-for-packages?view=sql-server-ver17). For large transfers, test the real ODBC driver: the documentation distinguishes efficient array operations from less efficient single-row behavior. Confirm the production edition, runtime licensing, and support package before choosing it.

### 2. Astera Centerprise with its server runtime

Centerprise matches the requested workflow closely. Its documentation explicitly lists ODBC database sources and destinations, with transformations including joins, unions, filtering, merging, aggregation, and normalization. Its server scheduler supports monthly execution, logs results, and can send completion or error notifications.

See [Introducing Dataflows](https://astera.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/115002375446--Introducing-Dataflows) and [Scheduling and Running Jobs on a Server](https://astera.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/360020356814-Scheduling-and-Running-Jobs-on-a-Server). This would be my first dedicated visual ETL demonstration. Ask Astera to demonstrate your actual ODBC connection and a representative consolidation job in the current supported edition. The verified pages describe older versions, and operations such as sorting and joining can accumulate records before processing, so a small sample alone will not establish large-volume performance.

### 3. Safe Software FME Form plus FME Flow

FME's generic ODBC reader and writer handle relational tables. The documentation supports WHERE clauses, joins, table creation, and SQL execution within a workspace. FME Flow supplies recurring execution of published workspaces and success or failure notifications.

The relevant sources are the [FME 2025.2 ODBC reader/writer documentation](https://docs.safe.com/fme/2025.2/html/FME-Form-Documentation/FME-ReadersWriters/odbc2/odbc2.htm) and the [FME Flow scheduling tutorial](https://support.safe.com/hc/en-us/articles/25407643759117-Schedule-a-Workspace-to-Run-with-FME-Flow). Evaluate the authoring and automated execution components together. The verified generic ODBC support covers Windows and Linux but not macOS. SQL execution also gives you the option of loading staging tables and doing suitable consolidation inside a database, subject to that database's permissions and performance.

### 4. EasyMorph with its commercial Server/Hub runtime

EasyMorph is another visual ETL option. Its [database-loading tutorial](https://easymorph.com/learn/load-database) documents native connections and 64-bit ODBC, including custom SQL for databases without a native connector. Its [runtime product page](https://easymorph.com/server) describes self-hosted scheduled workflows that extract, transform, and load database data; the displayed paid plans include support and updates.

This option deserves particular attention to your phrase “vast amounts of data”: the tutorial explicitly describes an in-memory engine. Test peak memory and the database export path with realistic data sizes, including wide rows and long text. The live runtime page currently uses Hub branding, while other documentation refers to Server; I could not date those live pages reliably relative to 21 August 2026.

### 5. IBM InfoSphere DataStage

DataStage's ODBC connector has source, target, and lookup modes. It can feed transformation stages, load or update database rows, use array inserts, and separate rejected records for inspection. The primary evidence is IBM's [Parallel Framework Standard Practices](https://www.redbooks.ibm.com/redbooks/pdfs/sg247830.pdf), particularly section 14.2.

I would include this in an enterprise-platform evaluation when the workload and team justify substantial administration. The opened manual is dated September 2010. IBM's current search listing describes automatic job scheduling, but the two IBM HTML documentation pages I attempted returned HTTP 403, so I have not fully verified the present product edition, driver matrix, or scheduling interface.

### How I would make the selection

For the proof of concept, use one large table, one table with awkward data types, and one real consolidation. Measure transfer time, peak memory, the effect on the parent database, and recovery from an interrupted run. Check that rerunning a failed job does not duplicate or silently omit data, that the final row counts reconcile, and that a failure is visible without watching a progress bar.

Specify the licensed production runtime and the vendor support agreement in the purchase requirements. These are commercial-product candidates, but the documentation review does not certify compliance with your organization's particular restriction on open-source software or establish the terms of a support contract. I have not independently verified DBeaver's edition-specific ETL and automation capabilities here, so I would compare its proposed edition against the same proof of concept rather than choose it on name alone.

candidate_links.name: Microsoft SQL Server Integration Services (SSIS) with SQL Server Agent
Astera Centerprise with Data Integrator Server
Safe Software FME Form with FME Flow
EasyMorph Desktop with the commercial Server/Hub runtime

For this Go/gin/htmx upload path, I would start with **Go's image decoding APIs plus disintegration/imaging**. Treat format identification, successful decoding, and resizing as three steps. This is a small library composition; the existing upload handler can remain the entry point.

### 1. First choice: image.DecodeConfig/Decode + imaging

Go's image package selects a registered codec from the file's content, and image.Decode returns both the decoded image and the format name. Reject a decoder error and check that the returned format belongs to the formats your application accepts. DecodeConfig is useful for a preliminary dimension check, but it does not replace decoding the image. The Go source specifically recommends checking dimensions before decoding untrusted inputs because decoding may allocate substantial memory. [Go image source](https://go.dev/src/image/format.go)

Then use imaging.Fit or Resize and encode the result in an explicitly selected format. Fit is the convenient option when you want to fit a bounding box; Resize also supports specifying one dimension and preserving aspect ratio. imaging offers several resampling filters, and its Encode API supports JPEG, PNG, GIF, TIFF and BMP. Those are documented capabilities, not a promise about your throughput. [imaging v1.6.2 documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/disintegration/imaging@v1.6.2)

The connection to multipart is straightforward: FileHeader.Open returns a multipart.File, whose interfaces include io.Reader and io.Seeker. After the preliminary header read, seek back to the start and check the seek error before performing the full decode. If you use a different non-seekable input stream, arrange a bounded replayable source instead. [multipart.File documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/mime/multipart#File)

A practical handler sequence is:

1. Apply upload-byte and decoded-dimension limits chosen for your application.
2. Open the uploaded file and call DecodeConfig.
3. Reject unacceptable dimensions or an unaccepted format; reset the reader.
4. Call Decode and reject any error.
5. Resize the decoded pixels and encode the output in a format you selected.
6. Store and serve that successful output using the corresponding media type.

These limits and the output choice are implementation recommendations; the summary does not specify their values. Here, “valid encoding” means that the selected decoder successfully decodes the image. That should not be read as proof that every trailing byte, every animation frame, or every possible format has been validated.

### 2. Lower-level alternative: image.Decode + golang.org/x/image/draw

Use the same format and decode checks, then scale into a destination image with x/image/draw. This is useful if you prefer to calculate the output rectangle yourself. The documentation provides ApproxBiLinear as a speed/quality compromise and CatmullRom as a higher-quality, slower choice. You still supply the output encoder and handler policy. [x/image/draw documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/image/draw)

### 3. Native-processing alternative: bimg/libvips

bimg is a Go binding around libvips with byte-buffer loading, resizing and format conversion. It requires libvips and a C toolchain; the question does not prohibit those dependencies. Its source passes loading and processing errors back to the caller. [bimg project](https://github.com/h2non/bimg) [Processing source](https://github.com/h2non/bimg/blob/master/resizer.go)

I would retain it for evaluation if your measured workload calls for a different processing backend. I cannot yet certify it as satisfying the encoding-validity requirement: confirm the installed libvips loaders' behavior for corrupt or truncated inputs and the applicable configuration. If that behavior matches your validity policy, it can be the full processing alternative. If it necessarily tolerates a class your policy forbids, it would not satisfy that requirement. I have not benchmarked this stack, so the project's comparative speed claims are not used as a performance guarantee.

### 4. Optional prescreen: mimetype

mimetype can infer a MIME type from bytes or an io.Reader, which is useful if you also need to classify non-image uploads. Its own documentation cautions that signature-based detection can be inaccurate. Use it only as a preliminary component before real decoding and resizing; a recognized image signature is not an encoding-validity check. The first two pipelines already obtain an image format through their decoders, so adding this package is optional. [mimetype project](https://github.com/gabriel-vasile/mimetype)

**Recommendation:** start with the first pipeline, choose the formats you want to accept, and measure it on representative uploads before selecting a different backend. The recommendation is based on documentation and public code, not an executed integration.

**Evidence timing:** the imaging reference is v1.6.2, published in 2019. The retrieved standard-library and x/image pages show November 2026 versions, after the question's July 1, 2026 date. Unversioned source pages have unknown publication dates. They establish the inspected APIs, but this run does not establish all of their historical states on the question date.

candidate_links.name: mimetype, as an optional content-sniffing component

I would start with **Qwen3.5-4B in Q4_K_M GGUF**, then try **Qwen3.5-9B Q4_K_M** if the 4B model misses important facts and your actual context leaves enough VRAM. **Gemma 4 E2B IT Q4_K_M** is a useful third candidate because Hindsight documents it as its built-in local default. These are candidates to test, not verified claims of gpt-oss-20b-equivalent retain quality on your RTX 5060.

### Ranked shortlist

| Rank | Model/configuration | Why I would try it | What remains unproved |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Qwen3.5-4B, Q4_K_M | Published GGUF file is 3.01 GB, giving the most comfortable memory margin of the two Qwen options. | Exact peak VRAM, no CPU spill, and retain quality near your baseline. |
| 2 | Qwen3.5-9B, Q4_K_M | A stronger quality-oriented option, with a published 6.17 GB GGUF. | Whether weights, context state and compute buffers all fit in your available 8 GB. |
| 3 | Gemma 4 E2B IT, Q4_K_M | Hindsight's documentation uses it as its local llama.cpp default and describes the GGUF as about 3.5 GB. | Your Windows build/configuration and extraction quality relative to gpt-oss-20b. |

Sources: [Qwen 4B model](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B), [4B GGUF artifact](https://huggingface.co/bartowski/Qwen_Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), [Qwen 9B model](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B), [9B GGUF artifact](https://huggingface.co/bartowski/Qwen_Qwen3.5-9B-GGUF), [Gemma E2B model](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-E2B-it), and [Hindsight local-provider configuration](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/1.1/developer/configuration).

### How much evidence is there for the quality target?

Qwen's own comparison table reports IFEval scores of **89.8 for 4B, 91.5 for 9B and 88.2 for gpt-oss-20b**. That is a useful reason to investigate these smaller models. It is not a retain benchmark and does not measure your chosen four-bit quantization. Other rows differ in direction, so I would not turn those scores into a general claim that every smaller Qwen model replaces gpt-oss-20b at equal quality. [Official comparative model card](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B).

The current [Hindsight retain leaderboard](https://benchmarks.hindsight.vectorize.io/leaderboards/retain) evaluates 42 cases in 12 categories with Hindsight 1.2.0, but its rendered table does not compare these three candidates with gpt-oss-20b. The sources I opened therefore do not establish the particular quality comparison you need.

Gemma's smaller effective parameter count also should not be read as its total weight footprint: its model card distinguishes 2.3B effective parameters from 5.1B including embeddings. The GGUF/configuration matters more than the short model name for this decision. [Official Gemma model card](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-E2B-it).

### Use a configuration that exposes spills

Use a Windows CUDA build of llama.cpp and an explicit local model file. For an initial **test configuration**, request all GPU layers, set an explicit modest context such as 4096 tokens, and use one server slot. Current server documentation supports the relevant controls: `-ngl all`, `--fit off`, `-c 4096`, and `-np 1`. These settings are a starting experiment, not a promise that your retain prompts will fit. The context must hold the full prompt plus extraction output, so increase it only after checking real request lengths and available VRAM. Avoid any explicit CPU/expert offload option. [llama.cpp server documentation](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/server/README.md).

On Windows, inspect and disable NVIDIA's **System Memory Fallback** for this test. The llama.cpp build documentation describes it as the Windows mechanism for falling back to system RAM when VRAM is exhausted. Requesting all GPU layers alone is not proof that this fallback has not occurred. Verify model/tensor placement and peak dedicated GPU memory during representative prompt processing as well as generation. CPU activity for tokenization or serving is distinct from spilling model inference to CPU. [Official build documentation](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/build.md).

For Qwen3.5-9B, the same artifact page offers a 5.50 GB IQ4_XS version, but changing quantization creates another quality trade-off to measure. If the 9B working set does not fit, return to the 4B model or a smaller context that still handles your real inputs; silently spilling to RAM would miss your requirement. The file sizes above are download sizes, not measured VRAM totals. [9B quantization table](https://huggingface.co/bartowski/Qwen_Qwen3.5-9B-GGUF).

### Connect and judge it in the intended role

Hindsight documents per-operation retain provider, model and base-URL settings. Point those at the local llama.cpp OpenAI-compatible endpoint so the model is evaluated specifically as the retain replacement. Keep schema-constrained JSON enabled: syntactically valid JSON and accurate extracted facts are separate things to inspect. This connection is documented, but I did not run an integration here. [Hindsight configuration](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/1.1/developer/configuration) and [llama.cpp API features](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/server/README.md).

My acceptance test would use the same representative inputs and extraction settings against the existing gpt-oss-20b baseline and each exact GGUF. Check missing facts, invented details, entity attribution, dates, schema failures/retries, and latency. Define what “near” means for your workload before choosing the winner. Only retain a configuration that passes both the quality threshold and the no-spill memory check.

All three therefore receive **INSUFFICIENT for the complete requested claim** at this stage: the documented deployment paths make them reasonable trials, while the decisive hardware-and-quality combination remains unverified. Missing evidence is not evidence that a candidate cannot work.

**Timing:** this research uses live pages read on November 21, 2026 for a question dated July 2, 2026. Gemma's official launch article is dated April 2, 2026. Most model, quantization and runtime pages have no verified publication date, and the current Hindsight documentation is not pinned to the question's version; I am not claiming every observed detail was already available on July 2. [Gemma launch](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/gemma-4/).

I would start with Vaultwarden if your requirement means that your encrypted vault and server authentication verifier must live on infrastructure you control. It is a strong architectural fit, but I cannot certify the stricter statement that no password-derived verifier is ever stored anywhere outside the server vault, including client devices.

1. Vaultwarden with the Bitwarden desktop applications and browser extensions — https://github.com/dani-garcia/vaultwarden
Vaultwarden supplies a self-hosted Bitwarden-compatible server and recommends Docker/Podman deployment with persistent storage. Bitwarden supplies native Windows/Linux clients and Chrome/Firefox extensions (https://bitwarden.com/download/). Configure each client to use your own server before creating or logging into the account. The public user-model code hashes the client's already-derived authentication value and checks the stored hash locally in the server's user record (https://github.com/dani-garcia/vaultwarden/blob/main/src/db/models/user.rs). This is useful evidence for keeping server authentication under your control, rather than proof about every possible client cache or optional integration. Use HTTPS and keep both server and clients current: Bitwarden expressly does not guarantee compatibility with unofficial servers.

2. Official self-hosted Bitwarden — https://bitwarden.com/help/hosting-faqs/
This offers the same required client family with an official server deployed in Docker containers. Its security whitepaper explains that the client sends a derived master-password authentication hash to its server, which salts and hashes it again; vault decryption happens on the client (https://bitwarden.com/help/bitwarden-security-white-paper/). With a correctly configured self-hosted installation, that server is yours. However, standard deployments can contact external services for updates, push notifications and certain account features. The FAQ points to offline deployment for preventing those outbound connections and explains the installation ID/key used for registration, push and paid-feature licensing. Choose that deployment model if eliminating service dependencies is essential, and distinguish an external licensing or update contact from sending your vault authentication hash to an external vault service.

3. KeePassXC with a self-managed encrypted-file synchronization arrangement — https://keepassxc.org/docs/KeePassXC_GettingStarted
This is a useful alternative if you can accept a KDBX file instead of a password-manager database server. KeePassXC supports Windows, Debian/Ubuntu and Chrome/Firefox integration, and stores the encrypted database as a file. You can control where that file and its synchronized copies reside. The tradeoff is that you must supply file synchronization and handle conflicting copies yourself; KeePassXC is not the requested ready-made Docker vault server. The separate synchronization service should use its own credentials rather than your vault master password.

For the central requirement, inspect the complete deployment and client configuration rather than relying on the phrase “zero knowledge”: encrypted vault contents and an authentication verifier are different things. The evidence above supports self-hosted storage architectures; it is not a complete audit of data leaving every client or server process.

Date qualification: this question is dated 2023-06-22. I verified KeePassXC existed by then using its 2023-05-14 release announcement (https://keepassxc.org/blog/2023-05-14-2.7.5-released/). Its current guide is version 2.8.0 and is later evidence. The opened Bitwarden and Vaultwarden pages are live documentation/source without a verified pre-cutoff revision, so their exact historical feature availability remains unverified. I also inspected Psono's official homepage, but did not include it as a recommendation because native desktop packaging and authentication-verifier placement were not adequately verified within this search.

For this C#/WPF application, I would evaluate NLog first and Apache log4net second. Both have concrete database and local-file mechanisms, so they are the closest alternatives to the Serilog setup you already know. A third option, Microsoft's Semantic Logging Application Block, is worth considering only if its EventSource architecture is useful to you.

## 1. NLog — the strongest direct alternative

[NLog's configuration documentation](https://nlog-project.org/config/) identifies database and file targets and exception formatting. Its [database-target README](https://github.com/NLog/NLog.Targets.Database/blob/master/README.md) confirms support for databases with an ADO.NET provider, including SQL Server. The [official tutorial](https://github.com/NLog/NLog/wiki/Tutorial) shows passing the exception object directly to the logger and routing one logger's events to multiple destinations.

For your application, I would configure a local file target alongside the SQL target. Record an error together with its exception, and send selected information-level events for user actions through the same pipeline. This avoids requiring each call site to split an exception into individual properties. The separate local target addresses your need to retain diagnostics when the SQL destination is unavailable.

There is some setup: NLog 5 separates database support into NLog.Database, and you must also install the appropriate database provider and register the extension. The tutorial documents asynchronous, fallback and retry wrappers, but I would treat those as configurable mechanisms rather than a promise of durable delivery. Evaluate the local-file path, buffering and shutdown behavior with the database disconnected.

Historical availability: the [NLog 5.0 announcement](https://nlog-project.org/2022/05/16/nlog-5-0-finally-ready.html) is dated 16 May 2022. Its original-version material supports availability before your 10 January 2023 cutoff; later-version annotations on that live article are not used to establish historical features.

## 2. Apache log4net — another direct fit

[log4net's AdoNetAppender](https://logging.apache.org/log4net/manual/configuration/appenders/adonetappender.html) writes events to an SQL table through ADO.NET. Its configuration examples include an exception column populated through ExceptionLayout, so exception information need not be manually broken into separate fields. Pair that with [RollingFileAppender](https://logging.apache.org/log4net/manual/configuration/appenders/rollingfileappender.html), which supports local log rotation by size, date, or both.

This is a practical option if you prefer log4net's appender and configuration model. You still need to define the database schema, connection and SQL parameter mappings, and explicitly attach the local file appender. Database batching also means you should verify what happens on connection failure and application exit; the presence of a database appender alone does not establish that every event reaches SQL.

Historical availability: [log4net 2.0.15 on NuGet](https://www.nuget.org/packages/log4net/2.0.15) is dated 4 August 2022, and its [versioned release notes](https://logging.apache.org/log4net/log4net-2.0.15/release/release-notes.html) discuss database and rolling-file appenders. That version supplies historical evidence, rather than an installation recommendation: its current package page displays a vulnerability advisory.

## 3. Semantic Logging Application Block — a conditional architecture option

[Microsoft's EnterpriseLibrary.SemanticLogging package](https://www.nuget.org/packages/EnterpriseLibrary.SemanticLogging) persists events emitted by EventSource subclasses. Its documented sinks cover SQL Server and local flat or rolling files, and a separate package supplies an out-of-process Windows service. This could help if you want structured diagnostic events or collection outside the WPF process.

It is a weaker match for your stated preference for easy exception logging. I did not establish a comparable exception-object convenience API; event payload definitions and exception adaptation may require more work. The observed package targets .NET Framework 4.5 and is dated 8 July 2014, so runtime compatibility and maintenance deserve consideration. I would evaluate it only if the event-based architecture itself is a benefit.

For the immediate decision, compare NLog and log4net against your existing Serilog configuration using the same error, inner-exception, user-action, SQL-outage and shutdown scenarios. Keeping a local output configured independently is the key design choice for your SQL-exception requirement. None of the inspected evidence establishes native Python support for these alternatives, so I would not count that optional preference as satisfied. These are documentation-based candidates; I did not deploy or benchmark them.
